title: Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet I: the theft of the Tablet of Destinies
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.10, Anzu, SB I) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: The Epic of Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet I: 117 of 201 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (4 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
A hymn to Ninurta introduces the poem. Anzu, set to guard Enlil's bath, seizes the Tablet of Destinies and flies off; the gods look for a champion, and Adad, Gerra and Shara refuse.

The Epic of Anzu tells how the lion-headed bird Anzu stole the Tablet of Destinies from Enlil, and how the god Ninurta, after other gods refused, defeated Anzu and recovered it. The Standard Babylonian version has three tablets. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/10/SB/I) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed manuscript with the most signs preserved there. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives. Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 117 of the 201 lines of the eBL edition (58%), from 4 tablets in the British Museum: K.7257 (Nineveh), K.3454 (Nineveh), K.22880 (Nineveh), BM.38797.

Lines not shown. 84 of the 201 lines of the eBL edition have no witness here with an open photograph: 22-a+32 (only on YBC.9842); a+33 (only on YBC.9842, Di.2258); a+34 (only on YBC.9842); a+35 (only on YBC.9842, Di.2258); a+36 (only on YBC.9842); a+37 (only on YBC.9842, Di.2258); a+38-a+47 (only on YBC.9842, IM.58821); a+48 (only on YBC.9842); a+49-a+54 (only on YBC.9842, Di.2258); a+55-b+57 (only on YBC.9842); b+110-b+124 (no manuscript preserves it); b+167-c+195 (only on YBC.9842); c+198 (only on YBC.9842); c+199-c+201 (only on IM.95180, YBC.9842). Lines that survive only on tablets whose photographs are not openly licensed (for example in the Iraq Museum, Berlin, Istanbul, Ankara, Philadelphia or private collections), or only on tablets whose eBL photograph does not show the lines, are omitted.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

translation.text:
1Son of the king of the inhabited world, splendid one, beloved of [Ma]mi,
2The mighty one will I ever sing, divine firstborn of [En]lil,
3Ninurta, the splendid one, beloved of Mami,
4The mighty one will I ever praise, divine firstborn of Enlil.
5Born (in) Ekur, leader of the Anu[nna-gods], Eninnu’s hope,
6Who waters paddock, garden, town, street, and city,
7Wave of battles, dancer (in combat), sash of valor,
8Whose tireless onset raging fiends dread,
9Hear the praise of the mighty one’s strength!
10It is he who in his fierceness defeated and fettered the mount of stones,
11Conquering soaring Anzu with his weapon,
12Slaying the bull man in the midst of the sea.
13Doughty, valorous, slaughterer with his weapon,
14Mighty one, impetuous, leader of battle and fray!
15Until then, no daises had been built among the Igigi-gods,
translation.scan_note: British Museum K.7257: obverse, the tablet's own lines 2' to 16'. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/10/SB/I) attributes SB I 1-15 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: one face of a fragment about 4 cm wide with about 15 lines, ink K.7257 on the right edge. Consistent with eBL's obverse 15. The English translates eBL's composite text: words in square brackets are restored, partly from other manuscripts, and may not be legible on this tablet.

translation.text:
b+58And assigned to all the [gods] their responsibilities.
b+59Destiny reversing so that Anzu would hold […],
b+60Enlil entrusted him with the entrance to the sanctuary he had finished.
b+61He being wont to bathe in pure waters in his presence,
b+62His eyes would look upon the trappings of supremacy,
b+63On his lordly crown, his divine apparel,
b+64On the tablet of destinies in his hands Anzu was wont to gaze.
b+65He was wont to gaze, indeed, at the father of the gods, divine Duranki,
b+66He resolved in his heart to make off with supremacy.
b+67Anzu was wont to gaze on the father of the gods, divine Duranki,
b+68He resolved in his heart to make off with supremacy!
b+69“Let me be the one to take the gods’ tablet of destinies,
b+70“Then I will appropriate for myself the responsibilities of all the gods,
b+71“I will have the throne for myself, I will take power over divine authority,
b+72“I will give orders to each and every Igigi-god.”
b+73His heart plotted the assault,
b+74At the entrance to the sanctuary, where he was wont to gaze, he was waiting for morn.
b+75When Enlil was bathing in the pure waters,
b+76Undressed, his crown set on the throne,
b+77He took hold of the tablet of destinies,
b+78He took supremacy for himself, [divine authority] was overthrown.
b+79Anzu soared off and [made his way] to his mountain,
b+80Awful silence befell, deathly sti[llness] reigned.
b+81Their father and counsellor Enlil was speechless,
b+82The sanctuary shed its divine splendor.
b+83The gods of the land converged, one after another, for a plan.

translation.text:
b+84Anu made ready to speak,
b+85Saying to the gods his children,
b+86“O gods, which one of you would slay Anzu?
b+87“Let him make his the greatest name in the entire inhabited world.”
b+88They summoned the Irrigator, Anu’s son,
b+89Plan in mind, he said to him,
b+90They summoned Adad, the irrigator, Anu’s son,
b+91Plan in mind, he said to him,
b+92“O mighty Adad, ferocious Adad, let your battle not turn back,
b+93“Blitz Anzu with your weapon.
b+94“Let your [name] be greatest among all the great gods,
b+95“You shall have no equal [among] the gods your brethren.
b+96“Let there be daises to you, let them be built,
b+97“Found places holy to you throughout the four [world regions],
b+98“Let your [holy places] come into Ekur.
b+99“[Show yourself pre-eminent] before the gods, for your name shall be ‘Mighty One’.”
b+100[Adad] answered the command,
b+101[To] Anu his father he said these words,
b+102“[My father], who would rush off impetuously to an inaccessible [moun]tain?
b+103“[Which] one among the gods your sons could defeat Anzu?
b+104“He took hold of the [tablet of destinies],
b+105“He took [supremacy] for himself, divine authority is overthrown.
b+106“[Anzu] soared off and made his way to his mountain,
b+107“His [command] has become like that of divine Duranki,
b+108“[He has but to speak, the one he cur]ses will turn into clay.”
b+109The gods were despondent [at what he said].

b+164it-tar-ru-[m]a {d}i₂-gi₃-gi₃ u₂-na-aš₂-ša₂-qu GIR₃+MIN-š[u₂]
b+165{d}nin-ši-ku₃ pa-a-šu₂ i-pu-uš#-ma i-qab-[bi]

translation.text:
b+148“Anzu soared off and [made his w]ay to his mountain.
b+149“His command has become like that of divine Duranki.
b+150“He has but to speak, the one he curses will turn into clay.”
b+151The gods were despondent at what he said,
b+152He turned away, he refused to go.
b+153The gods were spent and left off making proposals,
b+154The Igigi-gods, where they were sitting, were fuming in a turmoil.
b+155The lord of wisdom, who dwells in the depths, the resourceful one,
b+156Was devising an idea in his cunning mind.
b+157Ea devised wisdom in his heart,
b+158What he thought of in his mind he said to Anu,
b+159“Let me give a command and so find the god,
b+160“And then I will appoint Anzu’s conqueror in the assembly,
b+161“Let me be the one to find the god,
b+162“And then I will appoint Anzu’s conqueror in the assembly.”
b+163When the Igigi-gods [he]ard this speech of his,
b+164The Igigi-gods rallied, did homage to him.
b+165The Leader made ready to speak,
b+166[Saying t]o Anu and Dagan these words,

Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges of a tall tablet of several joined pieces, inks K.3454 on the side edge and DT.292 on the top edge (eBL: K.3454+K.3935+DT.292). The English translates eBL's composite text: words in square brackets are restored, partly from other manuscripts, and may not be legible on this tablet.
